title: The scheduler and StartNew
sub: TaskScheduler, the pool's queues, TaskCreationOptions and child tasks
cards/0/body:
A task that has a delegate does not start itself. It is handed to a task scheduler (TaskScheduler), which decides where and when to run it:

  • TaskScheduler.Default — the thread pool;
  • FromCurrentSynchronizationContext() — into the current context, for example the UI thread (last lesson);
  • ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair — a ready-made pair for limits: "no more than N at once" and "strictly one at a time".

Tasks from async methods and TaskCompletionSource have no delegate: they are not run but completed from outside — by the state machine builder (unit 3) or by your code via SetResult (unit 5). They need no scheduler.
cards/0/deep:
A custom scheduler derives from TaskScheduler and implements three methods: QueueTask (accept a task), TryExecuteTaskInline (may it run right now on this thread) and GetScheduledTasks (for the debugger).

Inlining happens, for example, on Wait() for a task that has not started yet: the waiting thread may run it itself instead of standing idle. One more detail: if there is no SynchronizationContext and TaskScheduler.Current is not Default, await resumes on that scheduler. Code under a ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair stays under it after await.
cards/1/q: Which task never goes through a TaskScheduler at all?
cards/1/options/0: A task returned by an async method
cards/1/explain: An async method's task is a promise without a delegate: the state machine builder completes it. The other three carry a delegate, and someone has to run it — that is exactly the scheduler's job.
cards/2/title: Task.Run is StartNew with the right settings
cards/2/body:
Task.Run arrived in .NET 4.5 as a shorthand for the most common case. It equals StartNew with three explicit decisions: no token, no child attachment (DenyChildAttach, covered at the end of the lesson), strictly the pool. And for an async lambda it also does Unwrap.

A "bare" Task.Factory.StartNew(work) differs in everything: scheduler Current (the trap from the last lesson), options None, no unwrapping. With an async lambda it returns Task<Task>, and the outer task completes at the first real await inside.

You need StartNew when you need what it offers: a custom scheduler, LongRunning, a state object without a closure.
cards/3/options/3: Does not compile: StartNew does not accept an async lambda
cards/3/explain: StartNew returned Task<Task>. The outer task completed when the lambda reached its first await and returned the inner task. await waited only for that. With Task.Run it would be about 1000.
cards/4/title: Inside the pool: the global and local queues
cards/4/body:
TaskScheduler.Default hands tasks to the thread pool. The pool has more than one queue:

  • the global queue — shared, FIFO. Work queued from outside the pool lands there: from Main, from the UI thread, from your own Thread. The timer service thread also queues timer callbacks there;
  • a local queue — one per pool worker thread. A task created inside a pool thread (Task.Run or StartNew from another task) goes to that thread's local queue.

Once free, a pool thread looks for work in this order:

  • 1. Its own local queue, from the end: the most recently added task first (LIFO). Its data is most likely still in the CPU cache.
  • 2. The global queue.
  • 3. Other threads' local queues, from the front — the oldest tasks. This is work stealing: an idle thread takes tasks away from a busy one.

Local queues remove the crowding around a single shared queue, but the order stops being fair: a thread that spawns subtasks runs them before requests that have long been waiting in the global queue. The PreferFairness option (next card) puts a task into the global queue even from a pool thread. How many threads the pool has and how quickly it adds new ones (MinThreads, SetMinThreads) was covered in unit 4.
cards/4/deep:
A local queue is a special structure (WorkStealingQueue in the sources): the owner pushes and pops at one end almost without synchronization, while thieves take from the other end under a lock. So the expensive synchronization is paid only on a steal, not on every task.

ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem(cb) goes to the global queue by default even from a pool thread; the local queue is chosen with the preferLocal: true overload. When there is a lot of work and few threads, the pool may add a thread, and that thread starts by stealing.
cards/5/q: A task on pool thread P calls Task.Run(Step1), Task.Run(Step2), Task.Run(Step3) in turn and finishes. The pool's other threads are busy. Which step does P take first?
cards/5/options/0: Step3: a thread works through its local queue from the end
cards/5/options/1: Step1: the pool's queues are strictly FIFO
cards/5/options/2: None of them: Task.Run always uses the global queue, and the steps wait behind everything
cards/5/options/3: None of them: a thread does not touch its own queue; the steps wait until another thread steals them
cards/5/explain: The steps were created inside a pool thread and went to its local queue. The owner takes from the end — Step3, then Step2 and Step1. If another thread freed up, it would steal from the front — Step1. If you need an order, do not rely on the pool's queues: await the steps one by one or pass the work through a channel.
cards/5/wrong/1: Only the global queue and stealing from the front of another queue are FIFO. The owner takes from its own queue at the end.
cards/5/wrong/2: Task.Run uses the global queue only when called from outside the pool or with PreferFairness.
cards/6/body:
Creation options are hints for the scheduler and rules for task relationships:

  • LongRunning — work that takes a long time. The default scheduler gives it a dedicated thread instead of a pool thread: the pool keeps its worker and does not have to wait to inject new threads. It is only a hint: a custom scheduler may ignore it. And the thread serves a single delegate: with an async lambda the delegate returns at the first real pause, the thread exits, and the continuations after await already run on the pool;
  • PreferFairness — put the task into the global queue rather than the local one, even from a pool thread: closer to first come, first served. It does not make the task any faster;
  • AttachedToParent and DenyChildAttach — task relationships, more on them below;
  • HideScheduler — inside the task TaskScheduler.Current looks like Default;
  • RunContinuationsAsynchronously — as with TaskCompletionSource in unit 5.
cards/6/deep: In the default scheduler LongRunning is literal: it creates new Thread(…) { IsBackground = true }, which runs one task and exits. Creating a thread means an OS object and a stack reservation, on the order of tens of microseconds or more. For short tasks the option hurts.
cards/7/q: How long does the dedicated thread allocated for LongRunning live?
cards/7/options/0: Until the first real pause at an await
cards/7/options/1: As long as the loop spins, i.e. forever
cards/7/options/2: Not at all: the option fails with an async lambda
cards/7/options/3: Until the garbage collector collects the task
cards/7/explain: The delegate is an async lambda. At the first incomplete await it returns a task, and the thread is free — so it exits. The loop continues on pool threads. The dedicated thread was created for nothing. This loop does not need LongRunning: it does not hold a thread anyway.
cards/8/body:
A task created inside a running task with AttachedToParent becomes its child:

  • the parent does not complete until all its children have. While it waits, its status is WaitingForChildrenToComplete;
  • children's exceptions end up in the parent's AggregateException.

Without the option a nested task is independent (detached): the parent knows nothing about it. This is the "structured parallelism" model of .NET 4.0. New code does the same explicitly: collect the tasks and wait with WhenAll.

Whether to attach is decided by the child, that is, by someone else's code. If a library creates a child with AttachedToParent inside your task, your task suddenly waits for foreign work and receives foreign exceptions. DenyChildAttach on the parent silently cancels such requests: the child becomes an ordinary independent task, without any error. Task.Run always sets it.
cards/8/deep: How it works: on creation a task checks which task is currently running on this thread. If AttachedToParent is set and that task has no DenyChildAttach, the parent's counter of unfinished children goes up. When the parent finishes its delegate, it decrements the counter for itself; each child decrements it on completion. Zero means the parent is complete.
cards/9/explain: The child is attached: Wait on the parent waits for it too. "parent" prints at once, "child" after 500 ms, and only then is the parent complete and "done" printed.
cards/10/q: The same code, but the outer StartNew is replaced with Task.Run, and the program waits for Enter at the end. What is printed?
cards/10/options/0: parent, done, child: the child did not attach
cards/10/options/1: parent, child, done: the child's option beats the parent's settings
cards/10/options/2: parent and InvalidOperationException: attaching is forbidden
cards/10/options/3: parent, done — and nothing more: Task.Run cancels the unattached child
cards/10/explain: Task.Run sets DenyChildAttach, and the child's AttachedToParent is silently ignored. Wait covers only the parent body: "parent", "done", and "child" after 500 ms. The process is still alive thanks to ReadLine, so the child gets to print.
cards/11/q: Hardware polling is a blocking loop that runs for hours. Give it a dedicated thread without touching the pool, strictly through the standard scheduler
cards/11/explain: LongRunning with the default scheduler gives a dedicated thread. Default so as not to depend on which task the code is called from.
cards/12/options/1: Task.Factory.StartNew without a scheduler takes TaskScheduler.Current
cards/12/options/2: Task.Run unwraps the Task<Task> from an async lambda
cards/12/options/3: A task created on a pool thread goes to that thread's local queue by default
cards/12/options/4: LongRunning guarantees a dedicated thread with any scheduler
cards/12/options/5: PreferFairness makes a task run faster
cards/12/explain: LongRunning is a hint: only the default scheduler turns it into a dedicated thread. PreferFairness changes the queue, not the speed.
cards/13/q: Match the option to its effect
cards/13/pairs/0/1: A dedicated thread instead of the pool
cards/13/pairs/1/1: The global queue instead of the local one
cards/13/pairs/2/1: The parent waits for this child
